newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Gold price seen at $1,650 by 2010, forecaster says.
newsitem.headline: Gold price seen at $1,650 by 2010, forecaster says.

text.p: Gold prices could rise to $1,650 an ounce in constant 1995 dollar terms by the year 2010, independent forecast J.A. Saiger told delegates at a conference here on Tuesday.

That would follow a first wave of inflation-driven price increases during 1997-1999 which would shoot the price to $500 at least and at best to $850.00, he said at the ABN-AMRO hoare Govett World Gold conference.
A recent Economist Intelligence Unit (EIU) publication forecast gold rising by three percent per year after inflation between now and the year 2010, he said.
Saiger quoting the EIU report said there was a 60 percent probability that the price would rise to $580 per ounce, expressed "in continuous 1995 U.S. dollars".
There was a 25 percent probability that based on a real after inflation annual rise, the gold price could be $850 by the same time.
He said a third possibility was a scenario in which (rated a 15 percent probability) that a gold price of $462 could be expected.
He said he believed that development of the gold price "mainly occurs in direct connection with the long-term U.S. monetary policy".
Increases in the gold price mainly coincided with inflation pushes instigated by the U.S. Federal Reserve bank between 1960 and 1980.

He noted that "the fateful hour for the gold price" was when the inflation rate increases faster than the (U.S.) Treasury Bond (T-bond) interest rate, the situation in real interest rates was worsening dramatically and negative real interest rates appeared.
"At this exact moment an escape usually started from financial assets into fixed assets. Gold investments have been especially favoured," he said.

Between 1966 and 1980 three inflation-push waves occurred. the U.S. inflation rate went from one percent to 15 percent; the T-bond interest rates went from four percent to 12 percent and the CRB commodity Index from 100 to 333.
At the end of that period the silver price rose to $50 from $1.25 and the gold price to $850 from $42.50.

During the disinflationary phase between 1980 and 1982, U.S. monetary growth rates were reduced to minus 1.3 percent from 12 percent and inflation came down to three percent from 15 percent and interest rates to six percent from 14 percent.
Meanwhile the gold price fell to below $350 from $850 and the silver price to $3.50 from $50.00.
Since the beginning of the Clinton administration in January 1993, the Fed has been on a long term inflation course, Saiger said.

Between the beginning of the administration and the first quarter of this year, U.S. M3 money supply increased by eight percent from a decline of 1.3 percent and "one may count on a sensible inflation push during 1997 and 1999/2000", Saiger said.
The inflation high could be expected in 1999/2000, he foecast.
That kind of inflation development "should shoot the gold price to at least $500 within two to three years and at best up to $850," he said.

He told delegates, "Previously there could nevertheless occur....considerable market uncertainties resulting in a last sell-off wave in gold and especially gold mines," resulting in unique buying opportunities, he added.

The second gold boom would be between 2003 and 2005. "For the final stage of the inflationary phase the Goldbrief-forecast (Saiger's newsletter) -- after the third and largest price increase -- expects a gold price of $1,650 in constant 1995 dollars,' he said.
During that time the U.S. consumer price index will triple which will be necessary to reduce the U.S. debt from a likely level of over 50 per cent to a more supportable 25 percent, he said.
Unlike the EIU gold price forecasts which appeared to favour steady growth, Saiger forecast "intense price increases in wildest fluctuations'.
That meant that "optimal timing" for all buying and selling orders will be of decisive significance for profit or loss in precious metals.
During disinflationary phases buying equities ranked among the best investments and precious metals are among the worst. In an inflation phase, the rankings were reversed.
Gold declines in inflationary periods were often accompanied by consider increases in the Dow Jones until the gold price broke out of its downtrend immediately followed by heavy stock market losses.
"For the gold decline in 1996/1997, this pattern could also be typical," he said.
--Brian Spoors, +44 171 542 7771
